one_liner: Research harness for the Keiser-Lemire 'lookup' SIMD UTF-8 validator, about 4-6x faster than the best scalar validator it tests.
what_it_does: Benchmarks and tests SIMD UTF-8 validation kernels: lookup2, lookup3 and lookup4 (the Keiser-Lemire algorithm), Zwegner's validator, the 'range' algorithm and 'basic' (the older fastvalidate-utf-8 algorithm). They run against scalar validators (Hoehrmann-style DFAs, Fuchsia's FIDL string check and its ASCII-skip variants, UTF8-CPP 2.3.4) on two real files and on synthetic input. Each kernel is exposed as fastvalidate::<arch>::<algo>::validate(pointer, length) returning an error_code: it answers valid or invalid only, with no position, decoding or transcoding. It is a research repository with a CMake build, unit tests and checked-in results, not a packaged library.
how_it_is_fast: The lookup algorithm classifies every byte together with the byte before it using three 16-entry pshufb/tbl table lookups: the previous byte's high nibble, its low nibble, and the current byte's high nibble. Each lookup returns an 8-bit mask of possible error classes (too short, too long, overlong 2/3/4-byte, surrogate, above U+10FFFF, two continuations), and ANDing the three masks keeps only the errors actually present. A second check uses saturating subtractions on the vectors shifted by 2 and 3 bytes to find positions that must be 3rd or 4th continuation bytes, and XORs that with the first mask. Errors are OR-accumulated with no data-dependent branches, and a 64-byte block that is all ASCII skips the checks, giving about 0.4 instructions per byte on the README's real files and about 1 on random multibyte input.
when_to_use: Reproducing or extending the Keiser and Lemire SPE 2021 results, or timing a new validator against lookup2/3/4, Zwegner, range and the older fastvalidate kernel on one harness with instruction and branch-miss counters.
Choosing a SIMD UTF-8 validation design before porting it to another language or runtime (the README notes the .NET port SimdUnicode came from it).
Studying the lookup algorithm in a small code base: src/generic/utf8_lookup4_algorithm.h is about 225 commented lines over a thin simd8 wrapper for AVX2, SSE and NEON.
when_not_to_use: Production validation: the README says 'research purposes only: not for production use' and the repo has no LICENSE file; simdutf ships the same algorithm with runtime CPU dispatch.
You need transcoding, the error offset, or UTF-16/UTF-32 work: the kernels only answer valid or invalid.
x86 machines without AVX2: on x86-64 the benchmark binds the haswell (AVX2) kernels unconditionally, with no runtime check, and the build uses -march=native.
Predicting cold-data throughput: every published number is a hot-cache best-of-N run on 0.6-1.8 MB files or 16 KiB synthetic buffers; DRAM-bound throughput is not measured.

integration.dependencies: none for the kernels; the benchmark fetches lemire/counters v3.2.0 via CPM and vendors UTF8-CPP 2.3.4
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.14+; GCC or Clang (-march=native) or MSVC (/arch:AVX2 on x64)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 (SSE kernels exist in src/sse but are not timed by the driver) and ARM64 NEON; the driver stops with #error on other platforms
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the lookup4 code read here has no mutable globals (its only static data is a const lookup table), and the checker state lives in a utf8_checker struct

gotchas: The headline ratios depend on which baseline is picked: 36x and 64x are against the plain Hoehrmann DFA (0.58 GB/s, a serial table walk). The strongest scalar baseline in the same 2026 README run, fushia_ascii2 (Fuchsia's validator plus the authors' 16-byte ASCII skip), reached 5.33 GB/s on hongkong.html and 6.14 GB/s on twitter.json, so lookup4 leads a good scalar validator by about 3.9x and 6.0x (derived from page data). On synthetic pure ASCII in results/skylake.txt, fushia_ascii4 reached 29.4 GB/s against 58.7 for lookup4avx (2.0x).

The utf8lib baseline (vendored UTF8-CPP 2.3.4) depends heavily on the build. On the same file with the same call it ran 22.9 instructions/byte and 0.51 GB/s in results/skylake.txt and 0.38 GB/s in the 2024 README (old Makefile, -O3 without -march=native), but 6.7 instructions/byte and 2.57 GB/s in the 2026 CMake build. fushia stayed at 6.6-6.7 instructions/byte across those runs, so the lookup-versus-utf8lib gap is 8x or 33x depending on which run is quoted, and newer UTF8-CPP releases are not measured.

Oracle flaw in the tests: the brute-force bit-flip test in tests/unit.cpp requires lookup3 to agree exactly with fidl_validate_string. As adapted in benchmarks/fushia.h, that function range-checks 4-byte sequences with code_point < 0xffff instead of < 0x10000, so it accepts the overlong F0 8F BF BF (U+FFFF); a Python model of the function found this is the only invalid 4-byte sequence it accepts. The benchmark timings are unaffected because every timed input is valid, but a bit flip that produces that sequence would abort the test against a correct lookup3.

The published tables cover AVX2 only and name no CPU: the README run (April 2026, about 3.5 GHz) gives no model, and results/skylake.txt (about 3.69 GHz) and results/rome.txt (about 3.4 GHz) are identified only by file name. The README table comes from the April 2026 CMake/counters driver, whose real-file section still prints lookup4/basic/range (lookup4avx etc. appear only in the synthetic section), so its row names are current, not stale. Zwegner's validator beat lookup4 on twitter.json in that run (41.0 vs 37.0 GB/s).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the listed simd-intrinsics siblings validate UTF-8. The catalogued simdutf, simdutf8 (Rust) and SimdUnicode (.NET) are the production forms of this algorithm, so use this repository only to benchmark or study lookup2/3/4 against Zwegner, range and the older fastvalidate ('basic') kernels on one harness.
verified_claims_summary: In the April 2026 README run (unnamed x86 at about 3.5 GHz, CMake Release with -march=native, compiler not stated, hot-cache best-of-N), AVX2 lookup4 validated hongkong.html (1.8 MB) at 20.9 GB/s and twitter.json (631 KB) at 37.0 GB/s. The baselines were a Hoehrmann DFA at 0.58 GB/s, Fuchsia's validator at 2.6-2.8 GB/s and UTF8-CPP 2.3.4 at 2.57 GB/s (about 8-64x), plus the best ASCII-skipping scalar variant at 5.3-6.1 GB/s (about 4-6x). The older results/skylake.txt shows 17.1 GB/s against 0.62 (DFA), 1.58 (Fuchsia) and 0.51 (UTF8-CPP).
status_note: Refreshed in April 2026 (CMake, CI, new README run) but explicitly research-only and without a LICENSE file, so reference-only; production users should take simdutf, which carries this algorithm.
